summary:
Dagestan stands under the national framework of Russia, whose statutes and enforcement practice apply throughout the republic; the national layer is carried separately.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) names the North Caucasus, including Dagestan, as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing, and assesses transgender people and visible advocates as at risk specifically.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. Its advisory flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai, warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons with the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan singled out, and states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He said the situation worsens year on year.
tangentialFactors:
In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Map, Russia, Dagestan included, scored 2%, among the lowest scores in Europe, with explicit bans and legal limitations that make legal gender recognition practically impossible.

The Canadian advisory places identity-based violence alongside a general security threat: the same republics named for attacks on 2SLGBTQI+ persons are named for frequent terrorist attacks, so exposure in Dagestan is not solely a function of visibility.

The UK Home Office document is a country policy note rather than a travel advisory, which gives its North Caucasus finding weight beyond journey planning: it is the assessment standard applied to claims from this region.
localsOnly:
North Caucasus SOS operates from exile, and its assessment is that private existence for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus can itself trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. The group reports that conditions deteriorate year on year.

No Dagestan-specific shelter, complaint avenue or protective body for trans residents was identified in the sources; the practical support available to residents appears to sit with exile-based groups rather than local institutions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Dagestan-specific legislative instrument was identified. The republic's dedicated reference material reproduces national-level provisions, which are carried by the national record rather than repeated here.

The sources give no Dagestan-specific incident counts, dates or outcomes for transgender victims. The Canadian advisory names violence against 2SLGBTQI+ persons in the republic without figures, and the UK note describes regional campaigns without a Dagestan breakdown; whether Dagestan-specific incidents are documented elsewhere remains unresolved.

Which areas require special permission from the Ministry of the Interior, and whether that requirement attaches to a given route, is not specified in the sources and is unresolved.

The frequency of terrorist attacks referenced in the Canadian advisory is stated qualitatively; no rate or period is sourced.
